messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 56

He is 33 and works as a prosecutor, a job that has long required him to move toward conflict with a steady voice and a prepared mind. Before the bombing, he thinks of himself as someone who can stay composed in rooms where other people fall apart. He is married, and he and his wife have built a life around schedules, court calendars, and the quiet routines that make a busy career feel manageable. The attack changes the shape of that life in an instant.

He was downtown on a weekday morning when the explosion occurred. He remembers the ordinary details first: the cold air, the coffee in his hand, the sense of being late. Then the blast throws him off balance, and the world becomes noise, dust, heat, and a pressure in his chest that he cannot immediately name. For a moment he cannot tell whether he is injured or only stunned. People are screaming. Windows are gone. Sirens arrive with impossible speed, and he moves through the scene on instinct, helping a woman sit down, calling out to a man who is bleeding, then realizing later that his hands were shaking so badly he could barely hold his phone.

In the days after, he returns to work because he believes that is what he is supposed to do. He tells himself that as a prosecutor he is trained to be rational, to keep a clear head, to keep moving. Instead, he feels as if the event has lodged inside him and will not stay in the past. He sleeps poorly from the beginning. At night he wakes with his heart pounding, certain for a second that another explosion has happened. He lies still, listening for sounds in the house, and his wife learns to wake gently so she does not startle him. He is grateful for her patience, but he also feels embarrassed by how often he jumps when she enters a room unexpectedly.

Soon his days become organized around avoiding reminders. He stops taking the route downtown. He notices that he is scanning storefronts, backpacks, parked cars, and crowded public places with a vigilance that leaves him exhausted. Large gatherings make him tense in a way he cannot explain to others, and he begins to choose seats facing exits. At work, he finds himself distracted during meetings and court appearances, especially when a loud bang from a closing door or a dropped binder sends a jolt through him. His mind goes blank at moments that should feel routine. He is ashamed of how difficult it becomes to concentrate on witness statements and case preparation, tasks that used to feel almost automatic.

He does not talk much about what happened. When coworkers ask, he gives short answers and changes the subject. He worries that if he describes the blast in detail he will become visibly upset, and he cannot bear the thought of losing control in front of colleagues. At home, he is often physically present but mentally elsewhere. His wife notices that he seems distant, irritable, and preoccupied. He snaps more easily over small things, then withdraws into silence, ashamed of the anger that rises so quickly. He feels disconnected from her even when they are sitting side by side, and this disconnection frightens him more than he wants to admit.

Images of the attack return without warning. Sometimes they come as flashes while he is in court, sometimes as vivid scenes when he is trying to fall asleep. He sees smoke, hears the sharp crack of the explosion, and feels his body react before his mind can remind him that he is safe. He avoids news coverage about terrorism and becomes angry when reports replay footage of the blast. Even hearing discussions about unrelated violence can bring a wave of nausea and an urge to leave the room. He is less interested in things he used to enjoy, including dinners out, exercise, and time with friends, because being out in public requires too much effort and attention.

Over time, he begins to notice that he is living in a narrower world. He checks locks more than once, sits with his back to walls, and keeps track of exits almost automatically. He feels tired all the time, as though his body has not stopped bracing itself since the day of the bombing. At the same time, he remains determined to function. He dresses carefully, arrives at work on time, and continues to perform his role competently enough that most people do not see how hard each day is. From the outside, he still looks like the steady attorney everyone expects. Internally, he experiences himself as changed, more fragile and more alert, as if the world has become a place where danger can arrive without warning and never fully leave.
